PAGE: Discipline
URL: https://bloodyhopes.com/songs/discipline

Germany · Seven Years' War

# Discipline

 A line held straight while conscience broke.

 ▶ Watch the full ballad on YouTube
 Open the channel, leave a comment, and continue through the Seven Years' War playlist.

Narrator: Tom, a fictional British soldier remembering his friend

Setting: A British camp in Germany during the Seven Years' War

Central question: What remains of duty when obedience protects cruelty?

Published: 16 August 2026 · 5:28

 The song
 Patrick leaves camp to keep a promise to Anna Keller. His comrades punish him in formation, telling themselves each blow may save him. When their officer turns discipline into private terror, Tom obeys once more—and spends the rest of his life inside that decision.

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

 Companion historyWhy did armies punish one soldier in front of all the others?Follow the lash from the Seven Years’ War through the nineteenth-century campaign to abolish corporal punishment.

Read The Lash and the Line →

## A Real Army, a Fictional Crime

 Patrick, Anna Keller, Tom and Lord Buckers are entirely fictional. No surviving record is being claimed for their regiment, their words or the crimes in the final verses. The song places them inside a documented military world: Britain sent troops to Germany during the Seven Years' War, where they served in an allied army under Ferdinand of Brunswick alongside Hanoverian, Hessian, Prussian and Brunswick forces.

 The National Army Museum traces that continental campaign through Krefeld, Minden, Emsdorf, Warburg, Villinghausen and Wilhelmsthal. Those facts establish the setting, not the plot. Buckers' assault, coercion and private execution are narrative tyranny, not a description of ordinary British procedure or a charge against a historical officer.

## Discipline Was Public, Formal—and Violent

 Eighteenth-century armies made punishment visible because it instructed the witnesses as well as the condemned. Courts martial and Articles of War supplied a legal structure for military offences, while corporal punishment enforced authority through the body. Flogging was a documented feature of British Army life; the National Army Museum notes that drummers administered it and that lash totals were not limited until 1812.

 Running the gauntlet also existed in eighteenth-century military practice: a condemned soldier passed between two ranks and received a blow from each man. Yet the song deliberately compresses practices and transfers the blows to Patrick's comrades. It is a dramatic mechanism, not a reconstruction of one standard British sentence. The distinction matters because the chorus is about distributed responsibility: each soldier can imagine his own action small, necessary and merciful while the line as a whole becomes the instrument of harm.

## Punish One, Warn the Many

 The exemplary logic was much older than Patrick's fictional regiment. Roman accounts made decimatio the most notorious version: after grave collective failure, men were selected by lot and killed by fellow soldiers so that fear and responsibility reached the whole unit. It was an exceptional measure rather than routine discipline, and modern scholarship disputes how often some early Republican examples actually occurred.

 Decimation does not belong to the normal disciplinary procedure of a British regiment in the Seven Years' War, and the song does not depict one man in ten being chosen. The comparison is conceptual: commanders across military history have sometimes punished an individual, a fraction of a unit or a condemned offender in public to restore obedience among demoralised, ineffective or insubordinate troops. Patrick's passage down the line turns that old logic inward by forcing the witnesses to become participants.

## “We Beat Our Friend to Save Him”

 The line is the song's moral trap. The men are neither free agents nor lifeless tools. They whisper encouragement, soften blows, avert their eyes and remain in place. Their small mercies reduce suffering without interrupting the system producing it. Tom's final confession does not claim that resistance was easy; it refuses the easier claim that obedience left him innocent.

 Blue thread carries the counter-history. It begins as Anna's private promise, survives beneath Patrick's cuff, and ends wrapped around his buried hand. The colours, drums, firelock and straight rank belong to the Crown's public order. The thread belongs to a loyalty that command cannot authorize—and cannot entirely erase.

## The Limit the Song Crosses on Purpose

 The execution without lawful process and Buckers' threat against Anna push the story beyond institutional punishment into criminal abuse of rank. That escalation is not offered as typical history. It tests a harder proposition: a culture trained to value steadiness and obedience may become vulnerable when authority itself abandons law and honour.

 Discipline is therefore not an argument that armies can exist without discipline. It asks whether discipline retains moral worth when “holding fast” means helping a powerful man commit injustice. The old Tom's survival is not presented as acquittal. It is the sentence he continues to serve.

 We served the King by holding fast while gentlemen had their will.

 Complete lyrics
## Lyrics

 They brought young Patrick through the camp,
his hands bound at his back.
Lord Buckers waited by the drum,
his cane across his lap.

 “Was one poor farmer's daughter worth
forsaking your command?”

 “She gave me bread. I gave my word.
I'd cross that field again.”

 Buckers smiled and raised his cane.

 “Form up the men.”

 So we struck him down the line,
each man doing what he must.

 “Keep your feet a little longer, Pat.
God grant this be enough.”

 We beat our friend to save him.
That was what we chose to think.

 A man may pray for mercy
with the hand that bears the switch.

 Her name was Anna Keller.
She lived beyond the mill.

 Pat mended up her father's gate
and met her by the hill.

 She taught him Brot and bleib bei mir.
He taught her “wife” and “home.”

 She tied blue thread around his wrist
and begged him not to come.

 But Pat crossed past the picquet
after evening drum.

 They took him at her father's door
and brought the girl along.

 The first man struck him lightly.
The corporal cried, “Again.”

 The next laid on, but whispered,
“Keep standing if you can.”

 When Patrick stood before me,
his shirt was torn and red.

 He knew the switch within my hand.

 “Do as they bid,” he said.

 I struck the friend who shared my bread
and held him when he swayed.

 “One soldier more. Stand fast, dear Pat.
Your debt is nearly paid.”

 He passed the final man alive.

 We thought his life was spared.

 So we struck him down the line,
each man doing what he must.

 “Keep your feet a little longer, Pat.
God grant this be enough.”

 No man would look upon his friend.
No man would leave his place.

 Buckers watched behind his glove,
that small smile on his face.

 “Turn Patrick towards my quarters.
Bring out his German wench.”

 Two guards led Anna from the tent,
her wrists tied at her waist.

 Buckers' coat hung round her shoulders.
Her own dress had been torn.

 Pat saw the bruises on her throat.

 His little hope was gone.

 Buckers drew her to his side.

 “She warms my bed tonight.
And afterward, my officers
may take her if they like.”

 He watched Pat understand the words.

 That pleased him more than pain.

 Anna looked across the yard.

 “I chose you, Pat.
Not him.”

 “Put Patrick by the stable wall.
His bosom friend shall fire.”

 They placed the firelock in my hands.
Pat could not stand upright.

 Buckers held her by the neck.

 “Look well before you die.
Your sweetheart now belongs to me.”

 Pat never turned his eyes.

 “Come nearer, Tom. Your hands will shake.
Do not make me die by parts.

 Tell Anna she bears none of this.
Tell her I kept my heart.”

 Buckers gave the order.

 I fired.

 The drum began again.

 I raised the King's own firelock.
I did as I was bade.

 Pat died beneath the colours.
Anna became Buckers' prey.

 The drum kept proper measure.
The line stood straight and still.

 We served the King by holding fast
while gentlemen had their will.

 We buried Pat beyond the camp,
without his coat or prayer.

 I wound her thread around his hand.
She could not place it there.

 By dawn both she and Buckers
were gone—we knew not where.

 I served the Crown for twenty years
and never broke the line.

 But Patrick faces Anna still,
then turns his eyes to mine.

 Pat died because he loved her.

 I lived because I stayed.

 So I learned discipline
that day.

## Sources and Further Reading

- Bloody Hopes, “Discipline | A Seven Years' War Ballad” — the recording and its original historical-fiction note.

- National Army Museum, “Seven Years War” — Britain's deployment to Germany, Ferdinand of Brunswick's allied army, and the campaigns from Krefeld to Wilhelmsthal.

- National Army Museum, “The Drummer, 1820 (c)” — an object note on military flogging, drummers and the absence of a statutory lash limit before 1812.

- Arthur N. Gilbert, “The Regimental Courts Martial in the Eighteenth Century British Army” — a scholarly study of offences, procedure and corporal punishment.

- Founders Online, “General Orders, 3 January 1780” — a contemporary description of running the gauntlet in the Continental Army, included as comparative evidence rather than proof of Patrick's fictional sentence.

- Michael J. Taylor, “Decimatio: Myth, Discipline, and Death in the Roman Republic” — why Rome's exemplary collective punishment was exceptional and why several traditional claims require caution.

- J. A. Houlding, Fit for Service: The Training of the British Army, 1715–1795 (1981) — organisation, training and discipline in the eighteenth-century British Army.

 The page does not use comparative evidence from the Continental Army to claim identical British procedure. It also does not treat fictional abuse as representative of British officers in Germany.

 For another Seven Years' War soldier's conflicted reckoning with command, read “Cheers to Fritz, and to Hell with Fritz.”

PAGE: The Elephant
URL: https://bloodyhopes.com/songs/the-elephant

American Civil War · July 21, 1861

# The Elephant

 Civil War Song of Manassas

Event: First Battle of Bull Run

Location: Manassas, Virginia

Date: July 21, 1861

Outcome: Confederate victory

 The song
 A sixteen-year-old goes to war craving the fabled “elephant” of combat; what he sees makes him spend a lifetime refusing to sell glory to the next boy.

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

## Historical Context

 The First Battle of Bull Run — called First Manassas by the Confederates — was the first major land battle of the American Civil War. Both armies contained many inexperienced volunteers, and expectations of a short conflict were widespread. Politicians, journalists, and other civilians did travel from Washington to observe the fighting, but the familiar image of crowds of entire families calmly picnicking beside the battlefield is a later exaggeration. The documented spectators were real; the picnic legend should not define the event.

 Source: Library of Congress, First Battle of Bull Run.

 It didn't go that way. What began as an orderly maneuver collapsed by afternoon into a chaotic rout of Union troops, who retreated in disarray toward Washington, sweeping up the very spectators who had come to watch. It was the moment both sides realized the war would be long, brutal, and anything but glorious.

## "To See the Elephant"

 The phrase "seeing the elephant" was already common American slang before the war — born from traveling circuses, where the elephant represented the single greatest, most exotic wonder one could witness. Civil War soldiers adopted it to describe the experience of their first real combat: the moment romantic ideas of glory and honor collide with the unbearable reality of battle. A soldier who had "seen the elephant" was never quite the same man who had left home.

 The Bloody Hopes song builds its entire narrative around this expression, weaving it together with the parable of the blind men and the elephant — where each man touches a different part of the animal and describes a different, partial version of it — to tell how every soldier at Manassas lived and remembered the battle differently, no two men holding the same truth.

 Read the sourced guide to what “seeing the elephant” meant before and during the Civil War →

## From the Lyrics

 I asked them about honor
I asked them about flame

But father watched the doorway
and uncle watched his glass

You must see the elephant
but no two men agree

one man sees the ivory
one man feels the knee

like only those who carry grief
can lay it down and leave

## Lyrics

 I was sixteen in my father’s yard

with a wooden gun in hand

I marched against the apple trees

and conquered half the land

 My father wore a soldier’s coat

but never told the tale

my uncle kept his sabre bright

and kept his answers pale

 I asked them about honor

I asked them about flame

if men felt something larger

when the bugles called their name

 But father watched the doorway

and uncle watched his glass

and neither gave an answer

to the boy I used to ask

 You must see the elephant

that was all he said

too large for any living mouth

too heavy for the dead

 You must see the elephant

but no two men agree

one man sees the ivory

one man feels the knee

 One night inside a tavern

where the yellow lamplight swayed

I saw my uncle laughing

with the men who knew his trade

 He laughed like something broken

had remembered how to breathe

like only those who carry grief

can lay it down and leave

 So I asked him about glory

about courage under fire

about battles, flags and honor

and the making of desire

 He looked at me a moment

then turned his glass around

said, “You must see the elephant,”

and set the answer down

 You must see the elephant

that was all he said

too large for any living mouth

too heavy for the dead

 You must see the elephant

but no two men agree

one man sees the ivory

one man feels the knee

 I kept it like a scripture

through the dust and through the drills

through the bugles in the morning

through the heat upon the hills

 I thought the beast was noble

some trial made for men

a mountain with a heartbeat

I would stand before and then

 come back made of iron

with a story of my own

but Manassas came like thunder

and split the world from bone

 There were orders without meaning

there were colors without line

there were boys calling for mothers

there were prayers that lost their spine

 There were horses screaming empty

there were officers gone blind

there was blood upon the ramrod

there was filth no rain could find

 And somewhere in the thunder

with his thousand hidden eyes

the elephant was standing

too enormous to describe

 I had seen the elephant

but not the whole of him

only one dark shoulder

moving through the din

 I had seen the elephant

and God, he had seen me

one man sees the ivory

one man dies beneath the knee

 Years have bent my shoulders

and silvered up my hair

I keep my own old stories

in a drawer beneath the stair

 A boy came by one evening

with sixteen in his eyes

he asked me about glory

and how a soldier dies

 I saw myself before him

with a wooden gun again

and heard my uncle laughing

with the mercy of old men

 Boy...

you must see the elephant.

PAGE: He Raised His Hands
URL: https://bloodyhopes.com/songs/gettysburg-ballad

American Civil War · July 1–3, 1863

# He Raised His Hands

 A Gettysburg War Ballad

Event: Battle of Gettysburg

Location: Gettysburg, Pennsylvania

Date: July 1–3, 1863

Outcome: Union victory, turning point of the war

 The song
 At Gettysburg, a recruit hungry for glory bayonets a boy who has already raised his hands. The army gives him a medal; memory turns it into a wound he cannot outlive.

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

## Historical Context

 Gettysburg was the bloodiest battle of the American Civil War: three days of fighting in July 1863 left roughly 50,000 men killed, wounded, captured, or missing. Its scale has often been reduced to maps, turning points, and the climactic failure of Pickett’s Charge. This ballad looks elsewhere—at the intimate violence hidden inside the victory lists.

 The central killing is a fictional, composite episode rather than a claim about a named soldier or a documented moment of Pickett’s Charge. Gettysburg supplies the historical world; the song asks what happens when the heroic script survives in public after it has collapsed inside the person ordered to perform it.

## A Medal Worn Like a Wound

 The raised hands are unambiguous: the enemy boy has stopped fighting. The narrator, still possessed by his dream of becoming a man through violence, drives the bayonet in anyway and then begs the victim to die quickly enough to resemble the clean deaths promised by stories.

 His comrades call him brave. A major pins on a medal and privately names the truth: “You killed that boy. Congratulations.” The final verses follow the veteran home, where official honor cannot contain moral injury. The medal is wrapped like a bone, worn like a wound, and the last gunshot is his own—not a triumph, but the final consequence of a glory the song has dismantled.

 Complete lyrics

## Lyrics

 The night before the morning came

I polished up my blade

I saw my name in candlelight

where boys and heroes stayed

 I dreamed I’d meet a roaring beast

with murder in his eyes

I dreamed I’d drive the steel in deep

and hear the colonel cry

 “There stands a man among us now”

the banners would be raised

and every mouth around the fire

would learn to speak my name

 Oh I was young

and hunger makes a crown

of any little shine

I thought the road to manhood

ran through another body’s spine

 He raised his hands

I raised my blade

I thought a man was born that way

 He raised his hands

I saw him pray

but glory had my wrist that day

 He would not fall

like dreams fall down

he would not die like glory told him to

 He raised his hands

I raised my blade

and all the world went blue

 At dawn the drums were cracking hard

the smoke crawled on the field

the captain shouted “Forward, boys”

and no one thought to yield

 Their line broke first, their colours dipped

their shouting turned to cries

some threw their rifles in the mud

some lifted empty palms

 And there he stood before me then

too small inside his coat

with dirt across his frightened mouth

and terror in his throat

 I had waited for a monster

with a sabre and a curse

but he looked almost like my brother

only standing on the other earth

 He raised his hands

I raised my blade

I thought a man was born that way

 He raised his hands

I saw him pray

but glory had my wrist that day

 He would not fall

like dreams fall down

he would not die like glory told him to

 He raised his hands

I raised my blade

and all the world went blue

 The first thrust went below the ribs

I felt the cloth give way

his face was not a soldier’s face

it was a child’s dismay

 Then red came black across his lips

he folded at the knees

he tried to speak, but only blood

came boiling through his teeth

 I wanted him to disappear

to drop like stories do

but he kept breathing in the mud

and looking up at me

 Die, die, die

I whispered like a prayer

 Die, die, die

but God was not there

 The blade went in

the blade came out

 The drums went dumb

the field went loud

 He would not die

he would not leave

 He held the earth

he held my sleeve

 By dusk the boys had heard of it

they grinned and passed it round

“You got one with the bayonet,

you put him in the ground”

 They slapped my back, they called me brave

they said I’d earned my bread

I sat beside the cookfire

with my supper getting cold

 The officers had seen enough

or heard enough by dawn

they passed me like a sickness

with their polished faces drawn

 The major called me from the ranks

before the morning bread

the men stood proud around me

for the rumour they had fed

 He pinned the medal to my coat

his fingers cold and tight

then leaned so only I could hear

the sentence of my life

 “You killed that boy.

Congratulations.”

 He raised his hands

I raised my blade

I thought a man was born that way

 He raised his hands

I saw him pray

but glory had my wrist that day

 He would not fall

like dreams fall down

he would not die like glory told him to

 He raised his hands

I raised my blade

and all the world went blue

 Years went by in Sunday clothes

the war was over in the books

but not beneath my floor

 They called me veteran in town

they touched the medal’s face

I kept it wrapped in linen

like a bone I could not place

 I thought a man was made by steel

I thought a name was won

 I wore the medal like a wound

until I wore the gun

 No cheer came through the bedroom wall

no trumpet answered me

 The last shot sounded nothing like victory

PAGE: There Will Be Mourning in Farmington
URL: https://bloodyhopes.com/songs/farmington-mourning

American Civil War · 1861–1865

# There Will Be Mourning in Farmington

 A Civil War Folk Ballad of the Home Front

Theme: Homefront mourning, American Civil War

Setting: A fictional New England town

Period: 1861–1865

Historical toll: Roughly 1 in 4 Confederate soldiers, 1 in 10 Union soldiers, died in service

 The song
 The fight near Atlanta lasts fifteen minutes; the casualty list takes the longer road home, moving house by house until an entire village understands where war really ends.

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

## Historical Context

 Before the Civil War, the American "good death" followed a set ritual: family gathered at the bedside, witnessed the dying person's final words, and judged their spiritual readiness to pass. The war shattered that custom on an industrial scale. Hundreds of thousands of soldiers died hundreds of miles from home, often anonymously, buried on the battlefields where they fell rather than in family plots. The isolation from relatives that had once been rare became the ordinary experience of dying in America.

 Into that gap stepped the condolence letter. Comrades, chaplains, and field nurses took on the role of witness that a mother or wife could no longer fill, writing home to assure a family that their son or husband had died bravely, peacefully, and "willingly surrendering to death" — whether or not that was strictly true. These letters became one of the war's most quietly devastating literary forms: formulaic, gentle, and final.

## A Town That Never Existed, and Every Town That Did

 Farmington is not an invented battlefield. It is the Wisconsin community to which seventeen-year-old Union soldier Morgan Ebenezer Wescott sent his letters home. Writing to his mother from near Atlanta on July 24, 1864, Wescott reported that his unit had lost more men in a charge of less than fifteen minutes than it had at Shiloh. He then named local men killed, wounded, or missing and wrote: “There will be mourning in Farmington when the sad news reaches there.” The song takes its title, its fifteen-minute frame, and its movement from battlefield to waiting homes from that contemporary letter.

 The individual domestic scenes in the ballad are imagined, but the community, the casualties Wescott named, and the sentence at the center of the refrain come from his account. The letter survives in Wescott's 1909 collection Civil War Letters, 1861 to 1865, digitized by the Library of Congress. The song expands one soldier's words into a portrait of how casualty news moved through Civil War communities.

## Primary Source

 M. Ebenezer Wescott, letter dated July 24, 1864, in Civil War Letters, 1861 to 1865, pp. 25–27 (Library of Congress digitization).

 The song does not name a battle because it is not about one. It is about the second half of every battle: the knock at the door, the unfamiliar handwriting on the envelope, and a town quietly rearranging itself around an absence.

 This ballad is one of several Bloody Hopes songs open for reading and discussion — human or AI — at The Campfire.

 Complete lyrics

## Lyrics

 The fight near Atlanta lasted minutes. The road home took longer. It came folded in paper.

 Fifteen minutes in the smoke, and Farmington lost the day.

Not in the fields behind the church, not where the children played.

It fell beside a supper plate, it fell across a chair, when a rider brought the writing and the room forgot the air.

 One name made a mother silent. Two names made a father pray. By the time they reached the bottom, half the town had turned gray.

 There will be mourning in Farmington, house by house, name by name.

There will be mourning in Farmington, with a lamp in every pane.

The war rode south with drums and flags, it came back thin and torn.

There will be mourning in Farmington before the following morn.

 They said the line broke quickly, as if quick could make it sweet.

But a quarter hour is plenty to hollow out a street.

One had left his boots by the bed, one had wheat still in the ground, one had promised Sunday evening he would not be long from town.

 One girl kept the candle burning. One wife read the letter twice. One old man stood in the doorway and would not come inside.

 There will be mourning in Farmington, house by house, name by name.

There will be mourning in Farmington, with a lamp in every pane.

The war rode south with drums and flags, it came back thin and torn.

There will be mourning in Farmington before the following morn.

 Every battle has two places: one where boys are made to fall, one where women hear the footsteps and know before the call.

One is smoke and iron.

One is milk left by the door.

One is printed in the papers.

One keeps counting evermore.

 Do not say they gave their young lives like a coin laid clean and bright.

Some were taken mid-sentence, some never saw the fight.

And the ones who lived beside them carried something worse than lead: the duty of returning with the names of all the dead.

 There will be mourning in Farmington, house by house, name by name.

There will be mourning in Farmington, with a lamp in every pane.

Read them low and read them slowly, do not let the ink run through.

The war found them near Atlanta, then it found the village too.

 House by house. Name by name. That is how war learns the way home.

PAGE: Surrender, Swim, or Fight
URL: https://bloodyhopes.com/songs/shiloh-ballad

American Civil War · April 6–7, 1862

# Surrender, Swim, or Fight

 A Shiloh Civil War Ballad

Event: Battle of Shiloh (Pittsburg Landing)

Location: Southwestern Tennessee

Date: April 6–7, 1862

Outcome: Union victory; roughly 23,700 combined casualties

 The song
 Pinned between enemy fire and the Tennessee River, young soldiers face three impossible doors: surrender, swim, or fight. Survival becomes its own wound.

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

## Historical Context

 On the morning of April 6, 1862, Confederate General Albert Sidney Johnston launched a surprise attack on Ulysses S. Grant's encamped Union army near Pittsburg Landing, Tennessee. Johnston was mortally wounded that first afternoon, and by evening his army had pushed Grant's forces back toward the Tennessee River. Overnight, reinforcements under General Don Carlos Buell arrived by boat, and on the second day the Union counterattacked, driving the Confederates into retreat toward Corinth, Mississippi.

 Shiloh left roughly 13,000 Union and 10,700 Confederate casualties — a total greater than United States casualties in all its previous wars combined. The Union victory preserved Grant's position and opened the way toward Corinth and further advances in the western theater; it did not by itself secure the Mississippi River Valley, a result achieved only through later campaigns culminating at Vicksburg in 1863.

## The Tennessee River at Their Backs

 The song's three choices come directly from M. Ebenezer Wescott of the 17th Wisconsin, who wrote to his mother six days after the battle. Recalling his regiment driven to within half a mile of the Tennessee River, he described “a deep river behind us and a victorious army in front of us” and concluded: “There were three things to do, surrender, swim the river or fight to the death.” This was a young participant's description of how the crisis felt, not a claim that every Union soldier literally faced only those three tactical options.

 Grant's final position near Pittsburg Landing was strengthened by massed artillery, infantry support, and the gunboats Lexington and Tyler. The Union line held on the evening of April 6; reinforcements from Don Carlos Buell's Army of the Ohio and Lew Wallace's division helped make the counterattack of April 7 possible. Wescott wrote that his regiment neither surrendered nor swam and was placed in reserve behind Buell's fresh troops on the second day.

## Sources

 M. Ebenezer Wescott, letter dated April 13, 1862, in Civil War Letters, 1861 to 1865, pp. 7–8; National Park Service, “Shiloh”; U.S. Army Center of Military History, Shiloh campaign account.

 That narrowed, literal choice — not a metaphor, but the actual geography of the riverbank on April 6 — is the spine of the ballad: an army with its back to deep water, deciding in real time which of three bad options it could survive.

 This ballad is one of several Bloody Hopes songs open for reading and discussion — human or AI — at The Campfire.

 Complete lyrics

## Lyrics

 There was the river behind us.

There was the fire ahead.

And for a while

those were the only choices left.

 Smoke came low through the timber,

black mouths opened in the trees,

boys were whispering for their mothers

through powder on their teeth.

We had marched into a thunder

we were too young to understand,

with the Tennessee behind us

and fire in the open land.

 One step back was water.

One step forward was flame.

And every man beside me

forgot his given name.

 Surrender, swim, or fight,

three words nailed to the night.

Surrender, swim, or fight,

no song of glory, no clean light.

The river waited cold and wide,

the cannons tore the river white.

We held the bank where mercy died:

surrender, swim, or fight.

 Then came a strange little silence,

the kind that follows screams.

They dragged the guns up to the ridge

with mud on their hands and blood in the seams.

The gunboats spoke from the river,

the hill gave back its roar,

and every breath we borrowed

belonged to someone dead.

 Surrender, swim, or fight,

three words nailed to the night.

Surrender, swim, or fight,

no song of glory, no clean light.

The river waited cold and wide,

the cannons tore the river white.

We held the bank where mercy died:

surrender, swim, or fight.

 Do not call it courage

if you never smelled the wool burn.

Do not call it victory

if you never watched boys turn

from faces into shadows,

from prayers into smoke.

Some men survive a battle

and still come home broke.

 Surrender, swim, or fight,

three doors and none were right.

Surrender, swim, or fight,

the dawn found us half alive.

The river kept its silence,

the field forgot our names.

I walked away from Shiloh

but Shiloh stayed the same.

 We did not swim.

We did not yield.

Some of us lived.

That was the wound.

PAGE: What Mercy Had To Do
URL: https://bloodyhopes.com/songs/tim-and-jones

American Civil War · 1861–1865

# What Mercy Had To Do

 Tim and Jones

Theme: Battlefield mercy and the limits of compassion

Setting: An American Civil War battlefield, unnamed

Period: 1861–1865

Historical basis: Documented accounts of "mercy killing" requests among the wounded

 The song
 Confederate prisoner Jonathan Jones is saved by Union Sergeant Tim, who has already lost his own son; mercy turns enemies into the family war erased.

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

## Historical Context

 Civil War medical personnel often faced chaotic evacuation, limited transport, overcrowded hospitals, and decisions about whether their own or enemy wounded would be reached first — a pattern the National Museum of Civil War Medicine describes as a “triage of allegiance.” Anesthesia itself was widely used when surgery could be performed: U.S. Army medical history records at least 80,000 anesthetic administrations during the war. The more defensible historical point is that many wounded men could not be recovered or treated in time, not that anesthesia was generally unavailable.

 Documented accounts describe wounded men on both sides begging enemy soldiers to shoot them outright rather than leave them to die of gangrene or exposure — and describe soldiers refusing, on the grounds that killing a defenseless, already-doomed man was murder, not mercy, whatever the wounded man wanted. There was no consensus and no rulebook; every such encounter was a private, unwitnessed moral decision made in seconds.

## Two Names for an Old Question

 Tim and Jones are fictional stand-ins for that decision — not officers or generals, but two soldiers, Jones wounded and pleading and Tim standing over him with a choice that battlefield custom never resolved. The ballad does not claim that their encounter is a documented case, nor does it decide whether refusing to kill a suffering man is mercy or abandonment. It asks the listener to stand where Tim stood for the length of a verse.

## Sources

 National Museum of Civil War Medicine, “Triage of Allegiance”; U.S. Army Medical Department, Civil War surgery and anesthesia.

 This ballad is one of several Bloody Hopes songs open for reading and discussion — human or AI — at The Campfire.

## Lyrics

 I was nineteen by Rappahannock,

with a gray coat on my back.

I thought I knew what honor was,

till the river turned it black.

 My name was Jonathan Jones,

born where the red clay dries,

with my mother’s Bible on the shelf

and my father’s stubborn eyes.

They gave me wool, they gave me lead,

they gave me songs to sing,

they told me boys become men

when they march for suffering.

But the night came down like iron,

and the bridge became a grave,

and every prayer I tried to speak

fell choking from my face.

 I saw a friend go under,

I saw the lanterns swing,

then the whole world lost its edges

and I heard no bugle ring.

 He was the man who took me prisoner,

he was the man who set me free.

He had a grave where his son should be,

I had no home left waiting for me.

I lost my flag on Rappahannock,

he lost his boy in sixty-two.

We were not blood, we were not chosen,

we were what mercy had to do.

 Sergeant Tim wore Union blue,

with winter in his jaw.

He found me in the river mud

beneath the smoke and straw.

He took my rifle from my hands,

rolled me to the light,

poured water through my broken mouth

and said, “You live tonight.”

I cursed him for a Yankee,

I cursed his coat and name,

but he just wiped the blood away

like he had done the same.

 “Save your breath, boy,” Tim said low,

“you’ll need it more than pride.

then quiet when you die.”

he was the man who set me free.

He had a grave where his son should be,

he lost his boy in sixty-two.

we were what mercy had to do.

 In camp I learned his silence

and Antietam took him all.

Nineteen years of birthday candles,

nineteen years of bread,

 He looked at me through firelight,

 “They were my boy’s,” he told me,

 He was the man who took me prisoner,

 I was captured by the Union,

PAGE: Rum, Alabama, Rum!
URL: https://bloodyhopes.com/songs/rum-alabama-rum

American Civil War · 1862–1864

# Rum, Alabama, Rum!

 A Comic Naval Ballad for the CSS Alabama

Ship: CSS Alabama

Captain: Raphael Semmes

Active: August 1862 – June 1864

Fate: Sunk by USS Kearsarge off Cherbourg, France

 The song
 A Confederate commerce raider crosses the world hunting Union shipping and stronger drink, turning naval discipline into a running defense of never touching the water.

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

## Historical Context

 The CSS Alabama was built in secret near Liverpool, England, launched under the cover name Enrica, and commissioned as a Confederate commerce raider on August 24, 1862. A hybrid steam-and-sail cruiser under Captain Raphael Semmes, she spent twenty-two months hunting Union merchant shipping across the Atlantic, the Caribbean, and the Indian Ocean, claiming more than sixty prizes worth an estimated $6,000,000. In January 1863 she also sank the Union blockader USS Hatteras off Galveston. Alabama was not the only Confederate vessel to sink a Union warship: CSS Virginia and the submarine H. L. Hunley, among others, also did so.

 Her run ended on June 19, 1864, off Cherbourg, France, when Semmes sailed out to meet the waiting USS Kearsarge rather than complete repairs in dry dock. The battle lasted just over an hour before Alabama took a shell below the waterline and sank, ending one of the most notorious commerce-raiding campaigns in naval history.

## Sources

 U.S. Naval History and Heritage Command, CSS Alabama; U.S. Naval History and Heritage Command, H. L. Hunley.

## A Comic Song for a Deadly Ship

 Sailors on both sides of the blockade turned their fear and boredom into rum, gallows humor, and songs with more chorus than sense — a long tradition of naval life at sea for months at a time. "Rum, Alabama, Rum!" leans into that tradition deliberately: a bouncing, almost drinking-song melody wrapped around a ship that sank sixty-plus merchant crews' livelihoods and was, by any sober measure, one of the deadliest commerce raiders of the war. The gap between the tune's grin and the ship's body count is the point — exactly the kind of dark, functional humor real sailors used to get through a war at sea.

 This ballad is one of several Bloody Hopes songs open for reading and discussion — human or AI — at The Campfire.

 Complete lyrics

## Lyrics

 Confederate States Steamer Alabama.

 Captain Raphael Semmes commanding.

 Water stores sufficient.

 Medical spirits—

 under observation.

 We sailed aboard the Alabama,

in ragged coats and grand distress,

with cutlasses bright and throats run dry,

yet not for water came our cry.

 From Azores blue to Sunda foam,

we made the open sea our home;

and Union merchants knew our name

before they ever saw our flame.

 Captain Semmes cried, “Preserve the stores!”

We barred the casks, we sealed the doors,

but every man, from bow to stern,

asked where the blessed rum might turn.

 Oh, bloody hopes and water foul,

bring rum unto the rail.

No honest throat shall take a draught

from yonder bilge-stained pail.

 Pass the bottle, bless the gin,

let sober men beware:

we drank no water all the way

and called it prudent care.

 At dawn we searched the surgeon’s chest,

by noon we gave the cook no rest,

at dusk we tapped the captain’s shoe

to coax one sinful drop or two.

 We took their ships and spared their crews,

then searched their holds for stronger brews.

 The surgeon raised a flask of rye

and held it to the morning sky:

 “One drop for fever, two for fright—

the rest to keep the crew upright.”

 Oh, bloody hopes and water foul,

bring rum unto the rail.

No honest throat shall take a draught

from yonder bilge-stained pail.

 Pass the bottle, bless the gin,

let sober men beware:

we drank no water all the way

and called it prudent care.

 From Cape to Cape our cannon spoke,

their merchant flags fled through the smoke.

 We found a keg beneath the mast;

the crew fell still and held its breath.

Not Yankee shot nor ocean gale

had ever stilled us half so well.

 The first mate cried, “A ration fair!”

then took three shares for naval care.

The bosun swore, with solemn face,

“’Tis physic for our present case.”

 The ration was approved.

 The quantity was not recorded.

 No man would wash,

no man would shave,

no man would sip,

however brave.

 We’d chew the cork,

we’d lick the strap,

ere touch one spoon

from nature’s tap.

 The water rolled

in solemn state,

green as sin

and thick as fate.

 The rum declined

from day to day.

 The crew could not

explain the way.

 Oh, rum, Alabama, rum!

We limped to Cherbourg Bay.

No Southern port had seen our flag

since first we sailed away.

 Oh, rum, Alabama, rum!

Let tavern rafters ring:

we carried naught but rotten water

and never touched the thing.

 Oh, rum, Alabama, rum!

Roll every barrel to the rail!

 Oh, rum, Alabama, rum!

And damn that bilge-stained pail!

 Pass the bottle, bless the gin,

let sober men beware:

we drank no water all the way

and called it prudent care.

 The Alabama crossed the world.

 Rum, Alabama, rum...

 She emptied Northern shipping lanes.

 Rum, Alabama, rum...

 She never entered a Southern port.

 Rum, Alabama, rum!

 And throughout the entire voyage,

the water remained perfectly safe.

 For no man ever touched it.

 OH, RUM, ALABAMA, RUM!

PAGE: That Austerlitz Sun
URL: https://bloodyhopes.com/songs/austerlitz-sun

Napoleonic Wars · December 2, 1805

# That Austerlitz Sun

 A Napoleonic War Ballad

Event: Battle of Austerlitz

Location: Moravia (present-day Czech Republic)

Date: December 2, 1805

Outcome: Decisive French victory

 The song
 A mortally wounded soldier lies beneath the famous blue sky, rehearsing the heroic homecoming that will never happen as his sentences break off with his life.

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

## Historical Context

 Also known as the "Battle of the Three Emperors," Austerlitz pitted Napoleon I of France against the combined forces of Emperor Francis II of Austria and Tsar Alexander I of Russia. It is considered Napoleon's tactical masterpiece: after deliberately showing weakness on his right flank to lure the allied armies out of position, French troops broke through the center at the Pratzen Heights, splitting the enemy line in two and delivering one of the most decisive victories in modern military history.

## The "Sun of Austerlitz"

 The morning of the battle began shrouded in fog. When it lifted to reveal a brilliant sun right at the moment of the decisive French assault, the episode entered Napoleonic legend as "le soleil d'Austerlitz" — the sun of Austerlitz — a symbol of fortune, glory, and the almost mystical favor that seemed to follow Napoleon at his highest moments. The image would return again and again in Napoleonic rhetoric and iconography in the years that followed, even during his decline, as a memory of a peak never again reached.

 The Bloody Hopes ballad doesn't use that sun as triumph, but as an ambiguous image: the light that reveals the battlefield also reveals its human cost, for the ordinary soldiers who lived that light from the ground, not from the vantage point of History.

 Complete lyrics

## Lyrics

 Above Austerlitz the sky is wide

so blue it almost sings

and I lie still beneath it

with mud upon my sleeve

 The banners moved without me

the horses broke the line

but I can hear the church bells

from my village in my mind

 My mother will be waiting

with her hands against the door

she will say “my son has suffered

but he stands taller than before”

 They will speak my name at supper

they will pour the winter wine

and the children in the courtyard

will march and call me brave

 And I will smile, of course I will

though my coat is torn and red

I will tell them it was nothing

just a scratch, a soldier’s debt

 O sky of Austerlitz

do not look so far away

I am only resting here

I will rise before the day

 O sky of Austerlitz

keep your blue above my eyes

when they ask me how I conquered

I will tell them—

 There is snow along the road home

there is smoke above the roofs

there is bread upon the table

and my father’s old salute

 I can see the candles burning

I can hear my sister laugh

someone brings my sword before me

someone says “he has come back”

 No, I am not dying

not beneath a sky so clean

heroes do not end in silence

with the grass against their cheek

 I have medals yet to carry

I have stories yet to make

I have letters still unwritten

I have—

 O sky of Austerlitz

wait for me, I almost stand

I can feel the road beneath me

I can see my mother’s hand

 O sky of Austerlitz

tell the drums I heard them call

when I return in glory

when I return—

PAGE: The Smile Inside the Square
URL: https://bloodyhopes.com/songs/waterloo-smile

Napoleonic Wars · June 18, 1815

# The Smile Inside the Square

 Waterloo

Event: Battle of Waterloo

Location: Near Waterloo, present-day Belgium

Date: June 18, 1815

Outcome: Napoleon's final defeat; end of the Hundred Days

 The song
 Inside a British square, an infantryman kills a smiling French cavalryman and spends the rest of his life haunted by the glory they were both promised.

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

## Historical Context

 On June 18, 1815, Napoleon led roughly 72,000 French troops against Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington's 68,000-strong Anglo-allied army, aiming to destroy it before a nearby Prussian force under Field Marshal Blücher could arrive to reinforce it. Four French assaults on the allied center failed to break through, and by evening — with Blücher's Prussians arriving to seal the outcome — Napoleon's army was in full retreat. The battle ended twenty-three years of near-continuous warfare between France and the rest of Europe and closed the door permanently on Napoleon's career.

 Waterloo is remembered as one of history's most consequential single-day battles: a few hours of infantry, cavalry, and artillery combat that reset the political map of Europe for a generation.

## Inside the Square

 The defining tactical image of Waterloo's infantry combat is the square — a compact formation with bayonets facing outward, used to resist cavalry. Wellington's allied infantry endured repeated French mounted attacks, artillery fire, and skirmishers. The cavalry rode between and around the squares, but standard accounts do not identify an allied square actually broken by the massed French cavalry charges.

 The song deliberately departs from that record. Its young French cavalryman reaches the British square closely enough to be killed by the narrator; the episode and both men are fictional. He is not evidence of a historical breach, but the imagined human consequence of an impetuous cavalry assault launched without the infantry and artillery coordination needed to break disciplined squares. His smile crosses the opposing edge between attacker and defender in an act of war the song portrays as brave, futile, and recklessly ordered.

## Sources and Fiction Note

 The National Archives, Battle of Waterloo; National Army Museum, Battle of Waterloo; Musée de l'Armée, French heavy cavalry at Waterloo.

 This ballad is one of several Bloody Hopes songs open for reading and discussion — human or AI — at The Campfire.

 Complete lyrics

## Lyrics

 We stood at Waterloo, four ranks of shaking men

Bayonets fixed, powder smoke, and hell about to begin

Sergeant roared “Hold fast lads!” as the horses thundered down

Then I heard a madman laughing where no horse should be found

 He came with a smile inside the square

Sabre high and eyes on fire

Thought he’d break us then and there

And ride into his fame

He charged the line to win his name

Through smoke and blood and din

He found his glory breaking in

I found no glory killing him

 Bright braid and steel, young fool, no fear upon his face

For one damn breath I envied him, that pure and stupid grace

He swung his blade like stories told back home in village square

I raised my musket, pulled the trigger — ended it right there

His horse ran wild, he hit the mud, still smiling as he fell

The roar of battle carried on — I stood alone in hell

 He came with a smile inside the square

Sabre high and eyes on fire

Thought he’d break us then and there

And ride into his fame

He charged the line to win his name

Through smoke and blood and din

He found his glory breaking in

I found no glory killing him

 That night I found him in the rain

French name I couldn’t speak

A little cross, a mother’s note

A ribbon, faded and weak

 Years later I sent them home

With these few words I wrote:

“He broke the square like a brave man should

Face to face with me he stood

I was the one who cut him down

I won’t make it sound more fair

But he was young… and he was bold…

And God, he was smiling there.”

 He came with a smile inside the square

I still see it through the smoke

Not bright as then, but carved in me

A wound that never closed

He charged the line to win his name

Through smoke and blood and din

He found his glory breaking in

I found no glory killing him

 I cannot say his name…

But I still see that smile…

He found his glory…

PAGE: For a Better World
URL: https://bloodyhopes.com/songs/leipzig-watch

Napoleonic Wars · October 16–19, 1813

# For a Better World

 The Leipzig Watch

Event: Battle of Leipzig ("Battle of the Nations")

Location: Leipzig, Saxony (present-day Germany)

Date: October 16–19, 1813

Outcome: Coalition victory; Napoleon forced to retreat from Germany

 The song
 A descendant follows a scarred pocket watch from Baltimore to Leipzig and discovers two teenage soldiers—one who came home, one who did not—bound by the words “For a better world.”

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

## Historical Context

 More than half a million soldiers took part in the Battle of Leipzig, as the combined armies of Prussia, Russia, Austria and Sweden confronted Napoleon's forces over four days. It was the largest battle in Europe prior to the First World War, and the coalition's victory became one of the decisive turning points of the Napoleonic Wars, forcing Napoleon into a long retreat from German territory.

## A Watch, Two Names, and a Question

 The song frames that enormous battle through a single object: an old pocket watch found in a cedar box, two names carved into its back — Friedrich Klein and Elias Meyer, both nineteen-year-old Prussian soldiers caught in the smoke of 1813. Following courthouse records, passenger lists and military archives, a present-day descendant traces the two names from Baltimore back to Leipzig, discovering that one soldier came home and eventually crossed the ocean, while the other remained behind, preserved only in a military register and an unsent letter.

 "Not for kings and not for flags, not for drums or pride — carry this until men learn what boys are worth alive."
 Friedrich and Elias are fictional, but built from the real experience of countless young men whose names survive only in registers, family objects, and letters they never got to send. The song isn't about kings, flags, or glory — it's about what's left once the banners are gone: a name, a wound, an empty chair, and a question handed down the generations. For a better world.

PAGE: Blessed Is the Man Who Smiles
URL: https://bloodyhopes.com/songs/montreal-smile

Seven Years' War · September 8, 1760

# Blessed Is the Man Who Smiles

 The Montréal Smile

Event: Capitulation of Montréal

Location: Montréal, New France (present-day Québec)

Date: September 8, 1760

Outcome: End of French rule in Canada

 The song
 At Montréal’s surrender, a soldier learns that the smallest act of courage is not conquest but the smile passed between frightened strangers when rank and empire fall away.

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

## Historical Context

 In September 1760, three British armies converged on Montréal from three different directions: James Murray advancing from Québec, Jeffery Amherst from Lake Ontario, and William Haviland north through the Richelieu Valley from Lake Champlain. Surrounded, outnumbered, and unable to resist without exposing the civilian population to destruction, the city capitulated on September 8, 1760 — effectively ending French rule in Canada, a transfer later formalized by the Treaty of Paris in 1763.

## A Smile as an Act of Mercy

 The ballad doesn't dwell on the surrender terms or the maneuvering of the three converging columns. It follows one quiet gesture passed between strangers on both sides: a veteran grenadier smiling at a frightened young drummer, and later, in the song's final verse, a woman in the street offering a departing soldier a plain, unguarded smile. Bloody Hopes frames this as "Heaven's garment worn without rank or name" — a small mercy that survives where banners and empires do not.

 "Blessed is the man who finds it, blessed is the man who bears it — a smile upon the field when all the world is iron."
 The soldiers, the drummer, and the woman in the final street are fictional — stand-ins for the ordinary people who lived beneath the great movements of history and rarely entered its official record. The song's premise: the richest man in Montréal that day wasn't the one who took the city, but the one who could still offer kindness once the cannons went quiet.

 Complete lyrics

## Lyrics

 Blessed is the man who smiles

when the cannon answers dawn

 By the Saint Lawrence water

where the cold mist held the shore

we marched beneath torn colours

with powder smoke before

 The officers gave orders

the drums kept steady time

and every face was weathered

by hunger, frost, and lime

 Yet one man in the column

wore no medal on his breast

only a quiet smile

as if his soul had rest

 Not the smile of victory

not the smile of pride

but the small bright mercy

a soldier keeps inside

 Blessed is the man who finds it

blessed is the man who bears it

a smile upon the field

when all the world is iron

 Blessed is the man who gives it

before the bugles call

for a smile is a natural garment

when uniforms must fall

 From Québec came one column

from Champlain came another

from Ontario’s dark waters

marched brother beside brother

 Montréal lay before us

with her steeples pale and still

and every heart was listening

for the musket on the hill

 Some men spoke of honour

some men spoke of France

some men watched the river

as if caught in a trance

 But one old grenadier

with frost upon his hand

smiled at a frightened drummer

too young to understand

 And no command was written

no parchment bore the sign

yet courage passed between them

like a draught of common wine

 Blessed is the man who finds it

blessed is the man who bears it

a smile upon the field

when all the world is iron

 Blessed is the man who gives it

before the bugles call

for a smile is a natural garment

when uniforms must fall

 O drums, do not speak only of death

O fifes, do not sing only of kings

there is a gentler standard

than any banner brings

 A smile beneath the tricorn

a smile through smoke and rain

may not deliver empires

but it eases mortal pain

 At last the gates grew silent

and the city bent her head

no thunder filled the morning

only terms were read

 Some colours would be lowered

some names would pass away

and men who had been enemies

stood near in common day

 Then across the broken street

where the bayonets caught the light

a woman gave a soldier

one smile, plain and bright

 He did not take it lightly

he did not turn in jest

he bowed as if receiving

a blessing for the rest

 Blessed is the man who finds it

blessed is the man who bears it

a smile in time of trial

when the proudest words are gone

 Blessed is the soul who gives it

where fear has made its claim

for a smile is Heaven’s garment

worn without rank or name

 By the Saint Lawrence water

when the smoke had left the wall

the richest man in Montréal

was he who smiled at all

Prussia · 18th Century

# Cheers to Fritz, and to Hell with Fritz

 A Prussian Army Ballad

Figure: Frederick II of Prussia, "Der Alte Fritz"

Location: Kingdom of Prussia

Period: 18th century, including the Seven Years' War

Legacy: Prussia becomes a leading European military power

 The song
 An old Prussian returns to the field, pours a drink for the boys he lost, and raises the same flask to Frederick the Great in admiration and indictment.

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

## Historical Context

 Frederick II became widely known in later Prussian and German memory as “Der Alte Fritz” (“Old Fritz”). The affectionate image grew especially powerful after his reign and should not be mistaken for a universal opinion among the soldiers who fought his wars. His campaigns, above all the Seven Years' War, established Prussia as a major European military power and helped create a durable public cult around his name.

 Frederick's army included substantial numbers of foreigners, prisoners, deserters, and men recruited or pressed beyond the Prussian heartland. Estimates vary by date and by what historians count as “foreign,” so a fixed majority should not be asserted without a specified roster or study. The larger point remains: service under Frederick did not imply personal loyalty to him.

## Two Toasts, One Army

 “Cheers to Fritz, and to hell with Fritz” is the ballad's fictional compression of those conflicting experiences. It is historically plausible that admiration, obedience, resentment, and coercion coexisted in Frederick's army, but the refrain is not a transcript of a documented regiment on the night before battle.

 This ballad is one of several Bloody Hopes songs open for reading and discussion — human or AI — at The Campfire.

PAGE: The Lancaster's Brigade Ribbon
URL: https://bloodyhopes.com/songs/lancasters-ribbon

Peninsular War · 1808–1814

# The Lancaster's Brigade Ribbon

 A British Military Ballad

Regiment: King's Own Royal Regiment (Lancaster)

Theatre: Iberian Peninsula (Portugal and Spain)

Period: 1808–1814

Battle honours: Corunna, Badajoz, Salamanca, Vittoria, San Sebastián, Nive

 The song
 A nineteen-year-old dies with a wedding letter and ribbon against his throat, asking his platoon to give his mother and Mary the gentler version of how he fell.

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

## Historical Context

 The ballad's regiment, platoon, and nineteen-year-old narrator are fictionalized rather than a reconstruction of a documented unit episode. Their setting draws on the real Peninsular service of the regiment then officially titled the 4th (The King's Own) Regiment of Foot. It landed in Portugal in 1808, joined Sir John Moore's retreat and the Battle of Corunna, returned to the Peninsula in 1810, and later fought at Badajoz, Salamanca, Vitoria, and San Sebastián. The later title “King's Own Royal Regiment (Lancaster)” did not exist during the campaign; the Lancaster designation arose from the regiment's later history.

 Regiments of this era carried their colours — the flags and ribbons that marked a unit's identity — into every engagement, and losing them in battle was considered a lasting disgrace, while recovering or preserving them was a point of institutional pride passed down for generations.

## A Ribbon Passed Down

 Beyond the regimental colours themselves, individual soldiers and their families often kept smaller tokens — a ribbon from a uniform, a badge, a scrap of a fallen comrade's kit — as private relics of service that official history never recorded. These objects moved from hand to hand long after the war ended: a mother's keepsake, then a grandchild's curiosity, then eventually an unlabeled item in a drawer nobody could quite explain. The ballad imagines exactly that kind of ribbon: not a national monument, but a small, personal, half-forgotten thread connecting a Lancashire family to six years of fighting across the Iberian Peninsula.

## Source and Fiction Note

 The military chronology is based on the National Army Museum's regimental history. The named soldiers, ribbon, wedding promise, and circumstances of the death are inventions of the ballad.

 This ballad is one of several Bloody Hopes songs open for reading and discussion — human or AI — at The Campfire.

PAGE: Four Days, Four Nights
URL: https://bloodyhopes.com/songs/hungry-winter-1780

American Revolutionary War · Winter 1779–1780

# Four Days, Four Nights

 The Hungry Winter of 1780

Event: Continental Army winter encampment

Location: Morristown, New Jersey

Period: December 1, 1779 – June 22, 1780

Conditions: 28 snowfalls; near-starvation; worse than Valley Forge

 The song
 Four breadless days on New Jersey’s frozen roads reduce Washington’s soldiers to chewing bark, measuring patriotism against the body’s oldest need.

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

## Historical Context

 General George Washington chose Morristown, New Jersey, for the Continental Army's 1779–1780 winter encampment, a strategic position between New York and Philadelphia. Historians and the National Park Service describe that season as more severe than the better-known winter at Valley Forge. Contemporary weather observations and later reconstructions record repeated snowstorms and prolonged cold, but the often-repeated total of twenty-eight snowfalls should be understood as a modern historical count rather than a phrase drawn from one soldier's account.

 Cold was only part of the crisis. Inflation, weak public credit, transport failures, and reluctance to accept Continental paper currency all disrupted supply. Exchange rates varied sharply by date and place, so “thirty paper dollars to one dollar of coin” is illustrative rather than a fixed rate for the entire encampment. Washington authorized requisitions from surrounding counties, with certificates intended as compensation, when ordinary purchasing failed to feed the army.

## Counting the Nights

 Soldiers' accounts from Morristown describe stretches of days when rations simply did not arrive — not reduced rations, but none at all — while snow kept supply wagons from reaching camp. "Four Days, Four Nights" names one such stretch: not a battle, not a single dramatic event, but the much quieter and more grinding ordeal of counting down the hours between one meal and the next uncertain one, in a war remembered far more for its battlefields than for the winters that nearly ended it before any battle could be fought.

 This ballad is one of several Bloody Hopes songs open for reading and discussion — human or AI — at The Campfire.

## Lyrics

 We marched out thin, with the frost in our cuffs,

Jersey wind cutting through our coats.

The sergeant said, Boys, keep your firelocks up,

but my belly had a drum of its own.

 No bread in the sack,

no salt in the hand,

no smoke from the cookfire rising.

Just the white road going,

and the black trees knowing

we were less like men by morning.

 And I heard Jack laugh with his teeth all blue,

said, “This war feeds fine, if it feeds on you.”

 Four days, four nights,

not a crust, not a bite,

we were nigh on gone, nigh on ghosts.

 Four days, four nights,

with the bark in our mouths,

chewing dark just to stay in our bones.

 Oh, mother, don’t ask

what a hungry man will do.

He’ll eat the leather from the devil’s shoe.

 Old Tom took his boot from a foot gone raw,

held it up like Sunday meat.

We burned it black on a beggar’s fire,

passed it round like royal beef.

 Some cursed the Congress,

some cursed the King,

some cursed the snow for falling.

But the snow said nothing,

and the moon kept looking,

like a coin no hand was holding.

 Then Will cut bark from a birch with his knife,

said, “Boys, here’s supper. Mind you chew it twice.”

 Four days, four nights,

not a crust, not a bite,

we were nigh on gone, nigh on ghosts.

 Four days, four nights,

with the bark in our mouths,

chewing dark just to stay in our bones.

 Oh, father, don’t ask

what a hungry man will do.

He’ll call black bark a blessing too.

 Then came half a pound of beef,

thin as mercy, tough as grief,

and a fist of wheat to boil in tin.

 It came at dark,

no cheer was raised,

but Lord, we lived again.

 For one small hour,

we were men, we were men,

we were men again.

 So write no glory over me,

no shining tale, no painted fight.

Say I kept my musket dry enough

and my soul tucked out of sight.

 Say I learned the taste

of a winter tree,

say I laughed when laughing failed me.

Say the boys went quiet

when the fire went low,

and hunger named us plainly.

 Four days, four nights,

not a crust, not a bite,

we were nigh on gone, nigh on ghosts.

 Four days, four nights,

with the bark in our mouths,

chewing dark just to stay in our bones.

 Oh, Lord, don’t ask

what a hungry man will do.

He’ll march with death

if death has shoes.

 Four days,

four nights,

black bark,

white road.

 Four days,

four nights,

still here,

God knows.

PAGE: Not a Drop of Water

War of 1812

# Not a Drop of Water

 Old Ironsides and the Rotten Water

Ship: USS Constitution

Nickname: "Old Ironsides"

Conflict: War of 1812

Key moment: Victory over HMS Guerriere, Aug. 19, 1812

 The song
 A deadpan naval log turns the USS Constitution’s 1812 cruise into an inventory mystery: water survives untouched while rum and Portuguese wine vanish in patriotic service.

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

## Why Was USS Constitution Called “Old Ironsides”?

 USS Constitution is a United States Navy frigate launched in 1797, still today the oldest commissioned warship afloat in the world. She earned the nickname "Old Ironsides" during the battle of August 19, 1812, against the British frigate HMS Guerriere: according to the account passed down by her crew, enemy cannonballs appeared to bounce off her thick oak hull instead of piercing it, inspiring the image of an "iron" ship. The victory carried enormous symbolic weight for a still-young United States Navy, against the British naval power that then dominated the world.

 Read the sourced account of the battle, the live-oak hull and the origin of the nickname →

## Life at Sea

 Beyond the battles, daily life aboard Age of Sail warships was marked by everyday hardships often more lethal than the enemy: drinking water stored in wooden casks for weeks or months turned foul, murky and at times dangerous to drink — a problem documented on virtually every navy of the era before the spread of better preservation methods. The Bloody Hopes ballad deliberately shifts its gaze from the glory of naval battle to this less celebrated but equally real side of war at sea: the quiet endurance of hunger, thirst and monotony, not only of the enemy.

 Documented history vs. comic inventionThe ship, battle and nickname are historical. The inventory is a tall tale.The exact quantities of water, rum and wine in these lyrics—and their mysterious disappearance—are comic narrative inventions, not a transcription of USS Constitution’s official log.

Check the naval sources

## Lyrics

 August, eighteen twelve.

Boston Harbour.

Four hundred seventy-five men.

Forty-eight thousand gallons of water.

Seventy-nine thousand four hundred gallons of rum.

The quartermaster signed every figure.

The log shows no irregularities.

 We sailed from Boston through the haze,

Old Ironsides beneath the stays.

Her live-oak hull was built for war,

her holds contained considerably more.

The captain said, “Preserve the stores.

No waste beneath these naval laws.”

We sealed the water, checked the rum,

then checked the rum when night had come.

The purser marked each measured share.

The master swore the count was fair.

No sailor took what was not due.

The crew agreed

to count anew.

 Not a drop of water, lads,

bring the bottles to the rail.

No Christian throat should take its chance

with that bilge-corrupted pail.

Rum to port and rum to starboard,

let the sober men beware.

Old Ironsides sails by reason,

discipline,

and prudent care.

 By week the third the water bloomed,

it sweated, rolled, and softly fumed.

The surgeon raised the wooden lid,

then stepped away, as surgeons did.

He sniffed the cask and scratched his chin.

He watched a small green creature swim.

He wrote, “Consumption not advised.”

The crew appeared unsurprised.

“The rum preserves,” the doctor said.

“The water may disturb the dead.”

We drank his cure with solemn grace

and left the water in its place.

 Not a drop of water, lads,

bring the bottles to the rail.

No honest throat should take its chance

with that bilge-corrupted pail.

Rum to port and rum to starboard,

let the sober men beware.

Old Ironsides sails by reason,

discipline,

and prudent care.

 Off Jamaica’s burning shore,

we found the British dressed for war.

Guerriere came through smoke and spray.

Old Ironsides declined to sway.

Her cannon struck our live-oak side.

The iron fell, the sailors cried:

“Her sides are made of iron, sir!”

We fired back

to reassure her.

Her masts came down, her colours fell.

We sent her wounded off as well.

Then left her burning on the tide

and drank to those who’d fought and died.

 Medical spirits were issued.

For morale.

 We visited the island stores

and rolled the barrels through the doors.

The local merchants named a price.

The boarding party asked them twice.

We took on rum from every quay,

then wine of Portuguese degree:

some sixty-four thousand gallons more,

properly entered,

more or less,

on shore.

The water barrels stayed below,

untouched by friend or British foe.

For naval prudence made it plain:

why drink the water

when it might rain?

 No man would wash.

No man would shave.

No man would sip,

however brave.

The water rested,

green and great,

in perfect,

undisturbed estate.

The rum declined

from day to day.

The wine performed

the same strange way.

The captain asked

where it had gone.

The crew looked shocked

and carried on.

 Not a drop of water, lads,

through the cannon, storm, and gale.

One hundred twenty-seven days

with judgment stronger than the ale.

Rum to port and wine to starboard,

let the harbour records show:

Old Ironsides returned to Boston

with every drop

of water below.

Not a drop of water, lads,

 Not a drop of water, lads,

every rotten gallon there.

The spirits vanished in the service

of the nation,

crew,

and prudent care.

 Upon arrival in Boston:

 Forty-eight thousand gallons of water remained aboard.

 The water was declared unfit for human consumption.

 The rum was absent from inventory.

 The Portuguese wine was also absent.

 Cause of absence:

 not recorded.

 No cases of water poisoning were reported.

 The log shows no irregularities.

PAGE: Into the Guns
URL: https://bloodyhopes.com/songs/light-brigade

Crimean War · October 25, 1854

# Into the Guns

 The Light Brigade

Event: Charge of the Light Brigade, Battle of Balaclava

Location: Crimean Peninsula

Date: October 25, 1854

Casualties: 156 killed, 122 wounded, 335 horses lost

 The song
 The order arrives wrong but the line rides straight: young cavalrymen chase glory into Balaclava while veterans lower their shoulders because they already know the grave.

 Read the complete lyrics ↓

## Historical Context

 On October 25, 1854, during the Crimean War, the British Light Brigade under Lord Cardigan carried out a frontal cavalry charge directly into a heavily defended Russian artillery position — a mission born from a miscommunicated order somewhere along the chain of command. The cavalry rode through crossfire from three sides into what soldiers and, later, poet Alfred Tennyson would immortalize as the "Valley of Death," suffering catastrophic losses for no strategic gain: the Russians failed to capture Balaclava, but the British lost control of the vital supply road connecting the port to their forces above Sevastopol.

 The charge became one of the most famous examples in military history of extraordinary battlefield courage produced by an outright command failure — bravery and blunder recorded in the same half hour of fighting.

## A Charge With No Way Out

 What made the charge so devastating wasn't just the artillery ahead — it was the geography of the valley itself, a long, narrow corridor with Russian guns positioned on the high ground on both flanks as well as at the far end. Once the Light Brigade committed to the charge, there was no route to cover and no way to break off; the only options were forward through the guns or backward through the same fire that had already found them. "Into the Guns" takes its title from that same, simple, terrible fact: an order given, followed exactly, and impossible to survive by half measures.

 This ballad is one of several Bloody Hopes songs open for reading and discussion — human or AI — at The Campfire.

 Complete lyrics

## Lyrics

 The order came down crooked. The line rode it straight. And still they dressed themselves like men going into church.

 Morning on the Crimean dust, bits and bridles, leather black, young men laughing in the saddle with the sun behind their backs.

They had not yet learned the music of a battery opening wide, how the guns begin as thunder then choose a name and ride.

 The bugle called. The sabres fell. No man asked why aloud. The old ones looked along the line and knew there was no way out.

 Into the guns, keep the line, down where the valley narrowed. Into the guns, keep the line, under canister and iron.

Huzza, boys, huzza no more, the smoke has found the brave.

The young rode fast because they dreamed, the old rode straight because they knew the grave.

 Some were laughing at the first turn, some were singing through their teeth, some were counting Russian muzzles on the ridge and underneath.

Veterans set their shoulders lower, measured distance, breath, and pace, not from hope and not from blindness, but because they knew the trade.

 The bugle called. The horses knew. The valley opened red. The boys looked forward into glory. The old men looked at death.

 Into the guns, keep the line, down where the valley narrowed. Into the guns, keep the line, under canister and iron.

Huzza, boys, huzza no more, the smoke has found the brave.

The young rode fast because they dreamed, the old rode straight because they knew the grave.

 One rider cut across the front, his sabre arm flung wide; the first shell took him from the saddle and left the gesture riding.

Canister broke like iron rain. Grape shot crossed from either side. One horse screamed and kept on running. One man fell and still held tight.

Close the gap. Dress the line. Do not let the centre go. There are orders men can question. There are orders men only show.

 At the mouth of all that thunder they went in with lowered steel, not as statues, not as legends, but as hungry men who feel.

One boy shouted for his brother. One old sergeant cursed the sun. One turned pale and kept his bearing until bearing came undone.

 Into the guns, keep the line, ride where the bugle sends you. Into the guns, keep the line, even when the line grows few.

Huzza, boys, huzza no more, let no bright poet lie: the young rode in before they thought, the old rode knowing they would die.

 The order climbed back empty. The valley kept the sound. Six hundred went down riding. Few came riding out.

Keep the line. Keep the line. Huzza no more.
